blocks.md: The monthly US household survey run by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (with the Census Bureau) to measure labour-force participation and employment. About 50,000–60,000 households a month.
The **March Annual Demographic Files** (now the ASEC) are the standard source for long-run wage inequality:

- The longest high-frequency series on participation and earnings in the US
- Reasonably comparable measures of the **prior year's** annual earnings, weeks worked and hours per week since 1964 — so earnings data start in **1963**
Processing changes over time affect, among other things:

- **top-coding** of high earnings
- flagging of **imputed** earnings
- algorithms for **allocating earnings** to non-respondents
- coding of **hours** worked per week
Any long-run series has to handle these breaks explicitly.

| Good for | Weak for |
| --- | --- |
| Wages by education, experience, gender | The very top — top-coding and under-sampling |
| Long annual series | Small cells, detailed geography |
| [Percentile Ratios](note:percentile-ratios), [Skill Premium](note:skill-premium) | [Top Income Shares](note:top-income-shares) → use [IRS Individual Tax Data](note:irs-individual-tax-data) |

sections.heading: May and Outgoing Rotation Group files (MORG)

blocks.md:
- **May CPS** supplements for 1973–1978, then the **Merged Outgoing Rotation Group** files from 1979: each month, households leaving the survey rotation are asked about earnings in their current job.
- They record **usual hourly or weekly earnings at a point in time**, rather than last year's annual earnings.
- A widely used cleaned version (May + MORG) is distributed by Acemoglu and Autor; the raw files are at the NBER (MORG) and IPUMS (May).

| | March CPS | May/MORG CPS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earnings concept | Last year's annual earnings | Usual hourly or weekly earnings now |
| Hourly wage | Constructed: annual earnings ÷ (weeks worked × usual weekly hours) | Reported directly for hourly workers |
| Hours data | Usual hours last year missing before 1976; noisy throughout | Point-in-time |
| Period | From 1963 | From 1973 |
| Best for | Long series, annual earnings, averages | The **distribution** of hourly wages |

For **average** wages both give very similar answers — measurement error averages out in large samples. For **dispersion** it does not ([Classical Measurement Error](note:classical-measurement-error)), so the choice of file matters for inequality.

- **Full-time, full-year** (FTFY) samples are common with March data but exclude many low-wage part-time and part-year workers, so they can mislead about the bottom of the distribution.
- The CPS — like the Census and the ACS — **top-codes** income ([Top Coding](note:top-coding)): measured variance is below the true variance and changes at the very top are invisible. For the top, use [IRS Individual Tax Data](note:irs-individual-tax-data) or the [SSA Master Earnings File](note:ssa-master-earnings-file).
